title: Six Core Human Needs
vimeoName: 6. Six core human needs - Master your reactions

segments.text: Most of us are fairly easy to understand
when things are going well.
The more interesting question is,
what happens when things are not going well,
when plans suddenly change,
when someone disagrees with you,
when work becomes repetitive,
when you feel overlooked,
or when you feel like you're not growing?
Pressure reveals something important.
It reveals the human need we're trying to protect.
Every one of us has six core human needs.
Certainty, variety, significance, connection,
growth, and contribution.
There is nothing wrong with any of them.
The challenge is recognizing them
before they begin controlling our behavior.
If certainty is important to you,
change can feel uncomfortable,
a new process, a different schedule,
an unexpected decision.
Your first reaction may be, why are we changing this?
Instead, pause.
Ask yourself, what do I know?
What don't I know?
And what's my next step?
Certainty doesn't come from everything staying the same.
It comes from knowing you can adapt.
Now think about variety.
If variety is one of your strongest needs,
routine may quickly become frustrating.
You may want to start something new.
Jump between tasks or change direction.
Ask yourself, do we really need a change?
Or do I simply need stimulation?
Sometimes change is the answer.
Sometimes finishing what you started is.
Creativity matters, but consistency creates results.
Now think about significance.
We all want to know that our work matters,
but when significance feels threatened,
feedback can feel personal,
disagreement can feel like rejection.
You may feel the need to defend yourself
or prove that you're right.
Pause and ask, am I solving the problem?
Or proving my value?
Real significance grows through reliability,
consistency, and the way you contribute every day.
Now think about connection.
If relationships matter deeply to you,
conflict can feel uncomfortable.
You may avoid difficult conversations
or agree simply to keep the peace.
Ask yourself, am I protecting the relationship
or avoiding discomfort?
Strong relationships aren't built by avoiding honesty.
They're built through trust, respect,
and open communication.
Now think about growth.
If growth drives you, repetitive work can feel frustrating,
but growth isn't always found in something new.
Sometimes it's found by improving what you already do,
working with greater skill, greater quality,
greater attention to detail.
Ask yourself, how can I grow through
what's already in front of me?
Now think about contribution.
Helping others is important,
but sometimes helping becomes taking over.
You solve problems that belong to everyone else.
You always say yes.
You carry more than your share.
Ask yourself, am I helping
or am I preventing someone else from growing?
Sometimes the greatest contribution
is teaching someone else to succeed without you.
Now notice something.
None of these needs are weaknesses.
They simply become visible under pressure.
The next time you feel frustrated,
defensive, impatient, distracted, or overwhelmed,
pause.
Ask yourself, which need am I trying to meet right now?
Then ask, is the way I'm meeting that need helping me?
Those two questions create choice.
Instead of reacting automatically,
you can respond intentionally.
Think about the last time you felt pressure at work,
which need felt threatened?
How did you respond?
And what could you choose differently next time?
Pressure will always be part of work.
Change will happen, feedback will happen,
challenges will happen.
The people who thrive aren't the people who avoid pressure.
They're the people who understand themselves
when pressure arrives.
Because the more aware you become of your own patterns,
the more freedom you have to choose a better response.
So the next time you notice yourself becoming frustrated,
pause.
Notice the need.
Choose your response.
Because every time you do,
you strengthen your emotional intelligence.
You become more resilient, more trusted,
a better teammate, and a better leader.
Awareness creates choice,
and better choices create better results.
